title: A method for comparing perceptual distances and areas with multidimensional scaling
author: Howson, Monahan

steps.title: Collect AX discrimination data
steps.instruction: Run an AX discrimination task with 25 participants using three rhotic segments (/r ɻ ʀ/) and three fricative segments (/z̪ ʐ ʑ/). Present each possible comparison for each segment six times per participant, yielding 210 trials (60 same‑comparison trials and 150 different‑comparison trials). Add 90 extra same‑comparison trials (15 of each same pair) to balance the design, giving 300 trials per participant (total 7 500 trials). Discard any response faster than 300 ms or slower than 2 300 ms, then compute d′ (d‑prime) values for each participant.

steps.title: Compute individual MDS coordinates
steps.instruction: For each participant, build a dissimilarity matrix from that participant’s d′ values and run a classical multidimensional scaling (MDS) solution in R using the cmdscale() function. Record the resulting six x‑ and y‑coordinates (one per object) for that participant; the unit of measure is perceptual units (p.u.).

steps.title: Average coordinates for plotting
steps.instruction: Across all participants, calculate the mean x‑coordinate and mean y‑coordinate for each object. Use these average coordinates to generate the final MDS plot (the alternative “standard” method would use a single MDS on the grand‑mean d′ matrix, but the protocol uses the averaged individual coordinates).

steps.title: Calculate pairwise distances
steps.instruction: For each participant, compute the Euclidean distance between two objects of interest using the modified Pythagorean formula: Distance = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)². Example distances: between /r/ and /ɻ/ and between /r/ and /ʀ/. Perform a statistical comparison of the two sets of distances across participants with a Student’s t‑test in R (t.test()), reporting the test statistic (e.g., t(47.87) = −0.87, p = 0.389).

steps.title: Compute triangle areas for groups
steps.instruction: For each participant, calculate the area of the triangle formed by the three rhotics (/r ɻ ʀ/) and separately the triangle formed by the three fricatives (/z̪ ʐ ʑ/) using the Shoelace (Surveyor’s) formula: Area = |x₁y₂ − y₁x₂ + x₂y₃ − y₂x₃ + x₃y₁ − y₃x₁|. Apply a Student’s t‑test to the two sets of areas across participants (e.g., t(24.93) = −72, p < 0.001).

steps.title: Calculate polygon areas (optional)
steps.instruction: When groups contain more than three objects, order the vertices clockwise or counter‑clockwise for each participant (provided orders: 1) /ʐ ʑ z̪ ɻ ʀ r/; 2) /ʐ ʑ ʀ r ɻ z̪/; 3) /ʐ ʑ z̪ ʀ r ɻ/; 4) /ʐ ʑ z̪ r ɻ ʀ/). Compute the polygon area with the generalized Shoelace formula: Area = | Σ_{i=1}^{n‑1}(x_i y_{i+1} − y_i x_{i+1}) + (x_n y₁ − y_n x₁) |, ensuring the polygon is non‑self‑intersecting. Example solutions (p.u.²): participant 1 = 16.95, participant 2 = 38.43, participant 3 = 16.05, participant 4 = 20.47. Statistical comparison can then be performed as desired.

description: Multidimensional scaling is a powerful tool used in psychophysics and perceptual research, among other fields; however, since its inception, there have been issues in accounting for variance across individual participants because of the general use of averages across all participants for the dissimilarity matrix. Previous researchers have suggested using individual MDS solutions to find general trends or patterns [16], but they have been limited in their usability because of the necessity of large datasets. Our method generates a set of coordinates for each individual participant which can be used for inferential statistics, increasing the power of the conclusions that can be made with an MDS analysis. This method is particularly useful in determining if there is a difference in two or more distances between objects or if the area occupied between two or more groups of objects is different. This provides a useful tool for asking theoretical questions about human perception.
